summary.text: At \(n=473165\), the number \(M=5292270077783=a(n)+4\) lies strictly between the two proposed consecutive values. It is Sierpiński because, for every exponent residue modulo \(48\), one of \(\{3,5,7,17,97,257,673\}\) properly divides \(M2^j+1\), and \(2^{48}\equiv1\) modulo each of these primes extends this finite covering to every positive exponent.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=9454129+11184810n.
\]
Recall that a Sierpiński number is an odd integer \(K>1\) such that, for every positive integer \(j\), the number \(K2^j+1\) is composite.

We disprove the conjecture by exhibiting one term \(a(n)\) for which there is another Sierpiński number strictly between \(a(n)\) and \(a(n)+28\).

Take
\[
n=473165.
\]
Direct multiplication gives
\[
11184810\cdot473165=5292260623650,
\]
and hence
\[
a(473165)=5292260623650+9454129=5292270077779.
\]
Set
\[
M=5292270077783=a(473165)+4.
\]
Thus
\[
a(473165)=5292270077779<M=5292270077783
 <5292270077807=a(473165)+28.
\]
It remains to prove that \(M\) is a Sierpiński number.

We use the covering primes
\[
\mathcal P=\{3,5,7,17,97,257,673\}.
\]
These numbers are all prime. For completeness, this follows by trial division by primes not exceeding their square roots. The relevant nonzero remainders are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
p&\text{remainders upon division by the primes at most }\sqrt p\\ \hline
5&5\bmod2=1\\
7&7\bmod2=1\\
17&17\bmod2=1,\quad17\bmod3=2\\
97&97\bmod2=1,\quad97\bmod3=1,\quad97\bmod5=2,\quad97\bmod7=6\\
257&257\bmod2=1,\quad257\bmod3=2,\quad257\bmod5=2,\quad257\bmod7=5,\\
&257\bmod11=4,\quad257\bmod13=10\\
673&673\bmod2=1,\quad673\bmod3=1,\quad673\bmod5=3,\quad673\bmod7=1,\\
&673\bmod11=2,\quad673\bmod13=10,\quad673\bmod17=10,\\
&673\bmod19=8,\quad673\bmod23=6.
\end{array}
\]
The primality of \(3\) is immediate. Thus none of the displayed numbers has a prime divisor at most its square root.

Every prime in \(\mathcal P\) divides \(2^{48}-1\). Indeed,
\[
2^{48}-1=281474976710655,
\]
and the following exact divisions hold:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
p&(2^{48}-1)/p\\ \hline
3&93824992236885\\
5&56294995342131\\
7&40210710958665\\
17&16557351571215\\
97&2901803883615\\
257&1095233372415\\
673&418239192735.
\end{array}
\]
Consequently,
\[
2^{48}\equiv1\pmod p
\qquad\text{for every }p\in\mathcal P.
\]

We now give a complete covering of all exponents modulo \(48\). The useful residues of \(M\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
p&M\bmod p\\ \hline
3&2=-1\pmod3\\
5&3\\
7&3\\
17&8\\
97&94=-3\pmod{97}\\
257&8\\
673&665=-8\pmod{673}.
\end{array}
\]
For example, these remainder statements can be read directly from the exact expressions
\[
\begin{aligned}
M&=3(1764090025927)+2,\\
M&=5(1058454015556)+3,\\
M&=7(756038582540)+3,\\
M&=17(311310004575)+8,\\
M&=97(54559485337)+94,\\
M&=257(20592490575)+8,\\
M&=673(7863699966)+665.
\end{aligned}
\]

Let \(r\) be any integer with \(0\le r<48\). We prove that one of the primes in \(\mathcal P\) divides \(M2^r+1\). There are seven cases.

1. Suppose \(r\) is even. Since \(2^2\equiv1\pmod3\), we have \(2^r\equiv1\pmod3\). Since \(M\equiv-1\pmod3\),
\[
M2^r+1\equiv(-1)(1)+1\equiv0\pmod3.
\]

2. Suppose \(r\equiv3\pmod4\). Since \(2^4\equiv1\pmod5\),
\[
2^r\equiv2^3\equiv8\equiv3\pmod5.
\]
As \(M\equiv3\pmod5\),
\[
M2^r+1\equiv3\cdot3+1=10\equiv0\pmod5.
\]

3. Suppose \(r\equiv1\pmod8\). Since \(2^8=256\equiv1\pmod{17}\),
\[
2^r\equiv2\pmod{17}.
\]
Because \(M\equiv8\pmod{17}\),
\[
M2^r+1\equiv8\cdot2+1=17\equiv0\pmod{17}.
\]

4. Suppose \(r\equiv5\pmod{16}\). Since
\[
2^{16}=65536=257\cdot255+1,
\]
we have \(2^{16}\equiv1\pmod{257}\), and therefore
\[
2^r\equiv2^5=32\pmod{257}.
\]
As \(M\equiv8\pmod{257}\),
\[
M2^r+1\equiv8\cdot32+1=257\equiv0\pmod{257}.
\]

5. If \(r=13\), then \(2^3\equiv1\pmod7\), so
\[
2^{13}=2(2^3)^4\equiv2\pmod7.
\]
Since \(M\equiv3\pmod7\),
\[
M2^{13}+1\equiv3\cdot2+1=7\equiv0\pmod7.
\]

6. If \(r=29\), repeated squaring gives
\[
2^8\equiv62\pmod{97},\qquad 2^{16}\equiv61\pmod{97}.
\]
Thus
\[
2^{29}=2^{16}2^8 2^4 2
 \equiv61\cdot62\cdot16\cdot2\pmod{97}.
\]
Here \(61\cdot62=3782\equiv-1\pmod{97}\), and hence
\[
2^{29}\equiv-32\equiv65\pmod{97}.
\]
Since \(M\equiv-3\pmod{97}\),
\[
M2^{29}+1\equiv(-3)65+1=-194=-2\cdot97\equiv0\pmod{97}.
\]

7. Finally, if \(r=45\), repeated squaring modulo \(673\) gives
\[
2^8\equiv256,
\qquad 2^{16}\equiv255,
\qquad 2^{32}\equiv417
\pmod{673}.
\]
Using \(45=32+8+4+1\), we obtain
\[
2^{45}\equiv417\cdot256\cdot16\cdot2\equiv589\pmod{673}.
\]
For clarity, the successive reduced products are
\[
417\cdot256\equiv418,
\qquad418\cdot16\equiv631,
\qquad631\cdot2\equiv589
\pmod{673}.
\]
Since \(M\equiv-8\pmod{673}\),
\[
M2^{45}+1\equiv(-8)589+1=-4711=-7\cdot673\equiv0\pmod{673}.
\]

These cases exhaust all residues \(r\) between \(0\) and \(47\). To see this explicitly, first every even residue is in case 1. An odd residue is either \(3\pmod4\), and hence in case 2, or is \(1\pmod4\). Among residues that are \(1\pmod4\), those congruent to \(1\pmod8\), namely
\[
1,9,17,25,33,41,
\]
are in case 3. The remaining ones are
\[
5,13,21,29,37,45.
\]
Of these, the residues
\[
5,21,37
\]
are \(5\pmod{16}\), so are in case 4, while the only residues left are exactly \(13,29,45\), handled in cases 5, 6, and 7 respectively.

We extend this finite covering to every positive exponent. Let \(j>0\), and write
\[
j=48q+r,
\qquad 0\le r<48.
\]
Choose the covering prime \(p\in\mathcal P\) supplied above for this residue \(r\). Since \(2^{48}\equiv1\pmod p\),
\[
2^j=2^{48q+r}=(2^{48})^q2^r\equiv2^r\pmod p.
\]
It follows that
\[
M2^j+1\equiv M2^r+1\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
Thus \(p\) divides \(M2^j+1\).

This divisor is proper. Indeed, every \(p\in\mathcal P\) satisfies \(p\le673\), whereas \(j>0\) implies \(2^j\ge2\), so
\[
M2^j+1\ge2M+1>673\ge p.
\]
Also \(p>1\), because \(p\) is prime. Hence \(M2^j+1\) has a divisor strictly between \(1\) and itself and is therefore composite. This holds for every positive integer \(j\).

Finally, \(M=5292270077783\) is odd and is greater than \(1\). Together with the preceding covering argument, this proves that \(M\) is a Sierpiński number.

We have therefore found, at \(n=473165\), a Sierpiński number \(M\) satisfying
\[
a(473165)<M<a(473165)+28.
\]
Consequently \(a(473165)\) and \(a(473165)+28\) are not consecutive Sierpiński numbers. The universal conjecture that this consecutiveness holds for every \(n\ge0\) is false.
